Moab rebels; Ahaziah becomes ill (verses 1–8)

When Ahaziah rebelled against the Lord, Moab rebelled against him.

Sin weakens us and brings us into poverty and distress.

A person's rebellion against God is often punished by the rebellion of those who owe that person obedience.

Ahaziah fell through a lattice or railing.

Wherever we are, there is only a step between us and death.

People call their homes their castles, yet no house can protect its occupants from divine judgment.

The whole creation groans under the weight of human sin.

Ultimately it, too, will give way under that burden, like the lattice through which Ahaziah fell.

No one is safe while making God an enemy.

Those who refuse to consult God's word to find comfort will eventually hear it as a warning of judgment, whether they wish to hear it or not.

Elijah calls down fire; Ahaziah dies (verses 9–18)

Elijah prayed for fire from heaven to consume the arrogant and defiant men sent against him.

He did not do so merely to preserve his own safety.

His purpose was to confirm his prophetic mission and reveal God's anger against ungodliness and injustice.

Henry explains that Elijah acted by an exceptional divine prompting.

But when Jesus' disciples wanted to do something similar, the Savior refused to permit it (Luke 9:54).

The gospel's dispensation of the Spirit and grace does not allow his disciples to act in that way.

Elijah was moved by concern for God's glory, whereas the disciples were defending their own reputation.

The Lord judges deeds according to the motives behind them, and his judgment is true.

The third captain humbled himself and appealed to the mercy of God and Elijah.

Nothing good can be gained by fighting against God.

Those who learn submission from the dreadful consequences of others' stubbornness act wisely.

The courage of faith has often frightened even the proudest sinners.

Ahaziah was so terrified by Elijah's message that neither he nor anyone around him attempted to harm the prophet.

Who can hurt someone under God's protection?

Like Ahaziah, many people expecting to prosper through sin are suddenly taken from this life.

Everything in this chapter warns us to seek the Lord while he may be found.
classic_reading:
[2Kgs.1.1-2Kgs.1.8]
2 Kings
Chapter Outline
The revolt of Moab--Sickness of Ahaziah, king of Israel.
(1-8)
Fire called from heaven by Elijah--Death of Ahaziah.
(9-18)
Verses 1-8
When Ahaziah rebelled against the Lord, Moab revolted from him. Sin weakens and impoverishes us. Man's revolt from God is often punished by the rebellion of those who owe subjection to him. Ahaziah fell through a lattice, or railing. Wherever we go, there is but a step between us and death. A man's house is his castle, but not to secure him against God's judgments. The whole creation, which groans under the burden of man's sin, will, at length, sink and break under the weight like this lattice. He is never safe that has God for his enemy. Those that will not inquire of the word of God for their comfort, shall hear it to their terror, whether they will or no.
[2Kgs.1.9-2Kgs.1.18]
Verses 9-18
Elijah called for fire from heaven, to consume the haughty, daring sinners; not to secure himself, but to prove his mission, and to reveal the wrath of God from heaven, against the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Elijah did this by a Divine impulse, yet our Saviour would not allow the disciples to do the like, [Luke.9.54] Lu 9:54. The dispensation of the Spirit and of grace by no means allowed it. Elijah was concerned for God's glory, those for their own reputation. The Lord judges men's practices by their principles, and his judgment is according to truth. The third captain humbled himself, and cast himself upon the mercy of God and Elijah. There is nothing to be got by contending with God; and those are wise for themselves, who learn submission from the fatal end of obstinacy in others. The courage of faith has often struck terror into the heart of the proudest sinner. So thunderstruck is Ahaziah with the prophet's words, that neither he, nor any about him, offer him violence. Who can harm those whom God shelters? Many who think to prosper in sin, are called hence like Ahaziah, when they do not expect it. All warns us to seek the Lord while he may be found.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesElijah divides Jordan.1–8Elijah is taken up into heaven.9–12Elisha is manifested to be Elijah's successor.13–18Elisha heals the waters of Jericho, Those that mocked Elisha destroyed.19–25
Elijah parts the Jordan (verses 1–8)

The Lord had made it known to Elijah that his departure was near.

He therefore visited the different schools of the prophets to give his last encouragements and blessing.

Elijah's departure pictured Christ's ascension and the opening of heaven's kingdom to all believers.

Elisha had followed Elijah for years.

He was unwilling to leave him now, when he hoped to receive a final blessing.

Let those who follow Christ beware of growing tired and giving up just before the end.

Long before, the Jordan had parted for the ark.

Now it parted before Elijah's mantle as a sign of God's presence.

For God's faithful people, death is like the Jordan they must cross to reach heaven.

Christ's death has opened a path through those waters for the redeemed.

O death, where are your sting, injury and terror?

Elijah is taken to heaven (verses 9–12)

The source of divine fullness from which prophets and apostles received their gifts still exists.

We are encouraged to ask God freely for abundant grace.

By faithfully attending Elijah, especially in his final hours, Elisha put himself in the position most suited to receive a greater share of his spirit.

What departing believers say about their experience of God can strengthen our resolve and brighten our own hope.

Elijah was carried to heaven in a fiery chariot.

Many questions about the event cannot be answered.

It is enough to notice what his Master found him doing when the hour arrived.

He was having a serious conversation with Elisha, encouraging and instructing him about God's kingdom among people.

We are wrong to imagine that preparing for heaven consists only of contemplation and acts of worship.

The chariot and horses appeared like fire, not burning but radiant and glorious.

Through the way Elijah and Enoch left the world, God gave a glimpse of the eternal life revealed in the gospel and the glory awaiting the bodies of believers.

It also represented Christ's ascension.

Yet even though Elijah entered heaven triumphantly, Israel could hardly spare him.

People who feel no sorrow when faithful and useful servants of God die have hard hearts.

Elijah's counsel, rebukes and prayers had protected the nation more effectively than its greatest military force.

Christ left the gospel with his disciples as Elijah left his mantle.

It is a sign of divine power working to overthrow Satan's rule and establish God's kingdom.

That same gospel remains with us, although the miraculous powers have been withdrawn.

It still has divine power to bring sinners to conversion and salvation.

Elisha receives Elijah's mantle (verses 13–18)

Elijah left his mantle to Elisha.

It represented the Spirit's gift and was worth far more than a fortune of gold or silver.

Elisha did not treat it as a sacred relic to worship.

He took it as a meaningful garment for use.

Elisha's question after Elijah's departure sought two things.

First, he sought God, the One to whom we may always turn when the human comforts we love are removed.

Second, he sought the God whom Elijah had served, honored and trusted.

The Lord God of the holy prophets remains the same yesterday, today and forever.

What use are the mantles, positions or books left by faithful people if we do not share their Spirit and their God?

Elisha parted the Jordan.

God's people need not fear the final crossing of death, because the Lord opens the way.

The sons of the prophets insisted on searching for Elijah, although the search was unnecessary.

Wise people may sometimes consent to a harmless but pointless request for the sake of peace and goodwill.

Yet searching hills and valleys will never bring us to Elijah.

Following his faithful and zealous example may, in God's appointed time, bring us to where he has gone.

Jericho's water healed; mockers judged (verses 19–25)

Elisha healed the water of Jericho.

Those who serve as prophets should make the places they visit better through their ministry, softening bitter hearts and making fruitless souls productive through God's word.

That word is like the salt Elisha put into the water.

The miracle pictured God's grace changing a sinful human heart.

Through the gospel, entire families, towns and cities have been transformed from wrongdoing to fruitful works of righteousness, to God's glory through Christ.

The young people of Bethel mocked Elisha as the Lord's prophet.

Their curse was not without cause.

They mocked him by saying “Go up,” referring contemptuously to Elijah's ascent to heaven.

Henry describes Elisha's curse as acting under an exceptional divine prompting.

He reasons that the ensuing judgment would not have followed unless the Holy Spirit directed that solemn action.

God is righteous, hates sin and will call it to account.

Young people should beware of wicked words.

God notices what they say.

They must not mock anyone's physical or intellectual limitations.

Mocking another person for doing good is especially dangerous.

Parents who desire true comfort from their children should teach them well from their earliest years and work to restrain the foolishness growing within them.

How terrible it will be for parents to discover at judgment that their bad example, carelessness or corrupt instruction contributed to their children's destruction!
classic_reading:
[2Kgs.2.1-2Kgs.2.8]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Elijah divides Jordan.
(1-8)
Elijah is taken up into heaven.
(9-12)
Elisha is manifested to be Elijah's successor.
(13-18)
Elisha heals the waters of Jericho, Those that mocked Elisha destroyed.
(19-25)
Verses 1-8
The Lord had let Elijah know that his time was at hand. He therefore went to the different schools of the prophets to give them his last exhortations and blessing. The removal of Elijah was a type and figure of the ascension of Christ, and the opening of the kingdom of heaven to all believers. Elisha had long followed Elijah, and he would not leave him now when he hoped for the parting blessing. Let not those who follow Christ come short by tiring at last. The waters of Jordan, of old, yielded to the ark; now, to the prophet's mantle, as a token of God's presence. When God will take up his faithful ones to heaven, death is the Jordan which they must pass through, and they find a way through it. The death of Christ has divided those waters, that the ransomed of the Lord may pass over. O death, where is thy sting, thy hurt, thy terror!
[2Kgs.2.9-2Kgs.2.12]
Verses 9-12
That fulness, from whence prophets and apostles had all their supply, still exists as of old, and we are told to ask large supplies from it. Diligent attendance upon Elijah, particularly in his last hours, would be proper means for Elisha to obtain much of his spirit. The comforts of departing saints, and their experiences, help both to gild our comforts and to strengthen our resolutions. Elijah is carried to heaven in a fiery chariot. Many questions might be asked about this, which could not be answered. Let it suffice that we are told, what his Lord, when he came, found him doing. He was engaged in serious discourse, encouraging and directing Elisha about the kingdom of God among men. We mistake, if we think preparation for heaven is carried on only by contemplation and acts of devotion. The chariot and horses appeared like fire, something very glorious, not for burning, but brightness. By the manner in which Elijah and Enoch were taken from this world, God gave a glimpse of the eternal life brought to light by the gospel, of the glory reserved for the bodies of the saints, and of the opening of the kingdom of heaven to all believers. It was also a figure of Christ's ascension. Though Elijah was gone triumphantly to heaven, yet this world could ill spare him. Surely their hearts are hard, who feel not, when God, by taking away faithful, useful men, calls for weeping and mourning. Elijah was to Israel, by his counsels, reproofs, and prayers, better than the strongest force of chariot and horse, and kept off the judgments of God. Christ bequeathed to his disciples his precious gospel, like Elijah's mantle; the token of the Divine power being exerted to overturn the empire of Satan, and to set up the kingdom of God in the world. The same gospel remains with us, though the miraculous powers are withdrawn, and it has Divine strength for the conversion and salvation of sinners.
[2Kgs.2.13-2Kgs.2.18]
Verses 13-18
Elijah left his mantle to Elisha; as a token of the descent of the Spirit upon him; it was more than if he had left him thousands of gold and silver. Elisha took it up, not as a sacred relic to be worshipped, but as a significant garment to be worn. Now that Elijah was taken to heaven, Elisha inquired, 1. After God; when our creature-comforts are removed, we have a God to go to, who lives for ever. 2. After the God that Elijah served, and honoured, and pleaded for. The Lord God of the holy prophets is the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever; but what will it avail us to have the mantles of those that are gone, their places, their books, if we have not their spirit, their God? See Elisha's dividing the river; God's people need not fear at last passing through the Jordan of death as on dry ground. The sons of the prophets made a needless search for Elijah. Wise men may yield to that, for the sake of peace, and the good opinion of others, which yet their judgment is against, as needless and fruitless. Traversing hills and valleys will never bring us to Elijah, but following the example of his holy faith and zeal will, in due time.
[2Kgs.2.19-2Kgs.2.25]
Verses 19-25
Observe the miracle of healing the waters. Prophets should make every place to which they come better for them, endeavouring to sweeten bitter spirits, and to make barren souls fruitful, by the word of God, which is like the salt cast into the water by Elisha. It was an apt emblem of the effect produced by the grace of God on the sinful heart of man. Whole families, towns, and cities, sometimes have a new appearance through the preaching of the gospel; wickedness and evil have been changed into fruitfulness in the works of righteousness, which are, through Christ, to the praise and glory of God. Here is a curse on the youths of Bethel, enough to destroy them; it was not a curse causeless, for it was Elisha's character, as God's prophet, that they abused. They bade him "go up," reflecting on the taking up of Elijah into heaven. The prophet acted by Divine impulse. If the Holy Spirit had not directed Elisha's solemn curse, the providence of God would not have followed it with judgment. The Lord must be glorified as a righteous God who hates sin, and will reckon for it. Let young persons be afraid of speaking wicked words, for God notices what they say. Let them not mock at any for defects in mind or body; especially it is at their peril, if they scoff at any for well doing. Let parents that would have comfort in their children, train them up well, and do their utmost betimes to drive out the foolishness that is bound up in their hearts. And what will be the anguish of those parents, at the day of judgment, who witness the everlasting condemnation of their offspring, occasioned by their own bad example, carelessness, or wicked teaching!

Jehoram rules Israel (verses 1–5)

Jehoram learned something from God's judgments and removed the image of Baal.

Yet he continued to support worship of the golden calves.

Those who abandon only the sins that have brought them obvious loss, while clinging to sins they expect to profit from, have not truly repented or reformed.

War with Moab; Elisha's intercession (verses 6–19)

Israel's king lamented the army's desperate lack of water and the danger it faced.

Yet he had summoned the other kings into the war.

Now he blamed Providence for the trouble.

Human foolishness corrupts our path, and then the heart becomes angry with the Lord (Proverbs 19:3).

Jehoshaphat did well to ask for the Lord's guidance, but he should have done it before entering the war.

Even good people sometimes neglect their duties until hardship drives them to perform them.

Wicked people often benefit from companionship with faithful believers.

Elisha told the kings to dig the valley full of trenches to receive water.

This tested their faith and obedience.

People expecting God's blessings should prepare to receive them—digging pools for promised rain, as in the Valley of Baca, making it a place of springs (Psalm 84:6).

There is no need to speculate where the water came from.

God is not restricted to ordinary natural causes.

People who sincerely seek the dew of his grace will receive it and become more than conquerors through it.

Water comes; Moab is defeated (verses 20–27)

It is a great blessing to live among people who are able to approach God through effective prayer.

A kingdom may survive and prosper because of the earnest prayers of those who are precious in God's sight.

We should esteem most highly the people whom he values most.

When sinners assure themselves that all is peaceful and safe, destruction may suddenly overtake them.

Despair then follows their reckless confidence.

Under Satan's influence, human beings have committed horrible acts that naturally make the heart recoil.

The king of Moab sacrificed his son in such a desperate and dreadful act.

It is wise not to drive even very wicked people to desperation when that can be avoided.

Rather, we should leave them to God's judgment.

[2Kgs.3.1-2Kgs.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
Jehoram, king of Israel. | (1-5) |
War with Moab, The intercession of Elisha. | (6-19) |
Water supplied, Moab overcome. | (20-27) |
Verses 1-5
Jehoram took warning by God's judgment, and put away the image of Baal, yet he maintained the worship of the calves. Those do not truly repent or reform, who only part with the sins they lose by, but continue to love the sins that they think to gain by.
[2Kgs.3.6-2Kgs.3.19]
Verses 6-19
The king of Israel laments their distress, and the danger they were in. He called these kings together, yet he charges it upon Providence. Thus the foolishness of man perverteth his way, and then his heart fretteth against the Lord, [Prov.19.3] Pr 19:3. It was well that Jehoshaphat inquired of the Lord now, but it had been much better if he had done it before he engaged in this war. Good men sometimes neglect their duty, till necessity and affliction drive them to it. Wicked people often fare the better for the friendship and society of the godly. To try their faith and obedience, Elisha bids them make the valley full of pits to receive water. Those who expect God's blessings, must dig pools for the rain to fill, as in the valley of Baca, and thus make even that a well, [Ps.84.6] Psa 84:6. We need not inquire whence the water came. God is not tied to second causes. They that sincerely seek for the dew of God's grace, shall have it, and by it be made more than conquerors.
[2Kgs.3.20-2Kgs.3.27]
Verses 20-27
It is a blessing to be favoured with the company of those who have power with God, and can prevail by their prayers. A kingdom may be upheld and prosper, in consequence of the fervent prayers of those who are dear to God. May we place our highest regard upon such as are most precious in his account. When sinners are saying Peace, peace, destruction comes upon them: despair will follow their mad presumption. In Satan's service and at his suggestion, such horrid deeds have been done, as cause the natural feelings of the heart to shudder; like the king of Moab's sacrificing his son. It is well not to urge the worst of men to extremities; we should rather leave them to the judgment of God.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesElisha multiplies the widow's oil.1–7The Shunammite obtains a son.8–17The Shunammite's son restored to life.18–37The miracle of healing the pottage, and of feeding the sons of the prophets.38–44
Elisha multiplies the widow's oil (verses 1–7)

Elisha's miracles were works of real charity.

So were the miracles of Christ.

They were not merely extraordinary displays of power but acts of great kindness to the people who received them.

God shows both his greatness and his goodness.

Elisha listened willingly to a poor widow's trouble.

People who leave their families burdened with debt often have little idea how much suffering they cause.

Everyone who professes faith in the Lord should trust him for daily provision without testing him through carelessness or wastefulness.

We should avoid running into debt.

Few practices bring more disgrace upon the gospel or leave more hardship for surviving family members.

Elisha helped the widow find a way to pay what she owed and support herself and her children.

The provision was miraculous.

But it also illustrated a wise ordinary way of helping distressed people: assist them in using what little they possess through their own diligent work.

The oil continued flowing while empty containers remained.

There is no shortage in God or in the riches of his grace.

The limitations are in ourselves: our faith fails, not his promise.

He gives more than we ask.

If more containers had been provided, there was sufficient oil to fill them.

God has enough for all and enough for each.

The Redeemer is sufficient to provide salvation for every sinner who comes to him, and his saving resources will not be exhausted.

The widow was to pay her debt first, before using the remainder to provide for the children.

Though her creditors had been harsh, the debt remained due.

One of the chief duties of Christian living is to pay every just debt and give each person what rightly belongs to them, even if doing so leaves little for ourselves.

We should act from conscience, not merely compulsion.

Honest people cannot comfortably enjoy their daily bread unless it is truly theirs.

Then the widow and her family could live on what remained, using the proceeds from the oil to support an honest livelihood.

We should not expect miracles of this kind today.

But we can expect God's mercy as we seek him and wait upon him.

Widows in particular may trust the Lord who rules human hearts and can provide just as effectively without an outward miracle.

The Shunammite woman is given a son (verses 8–17)

Elisha had earned the king's regard through his past service.

Yet a good person can find just as much happiness in serving others as in gaining influence or raising personal status.

The Shunammite woman did not require a favor from the king.

She was content to live among her own people, who loved and respected her and whom she could help.

Many people would be happier if they could recognize when their situation is already good.

God sees even a secret desire that we have held back in submission to his will.

He may hear the prayers of his servants on behalf of those who have helped them and send blessings that were neither requested nor expected.

The promises made by God's true servants must not be treated as mere attempts to flatter or deceive, like worldly promises.

The Shunammite's son is restored to life (verses 18–37)

The child died suddenly.

All a mother's tenderness could not preserve the life of a child who had come through promise and prayer and been received as a gift of love.

Yet the mother's restraint under this terrible suffering was remarkable.

She did not utter a bitter or irritable word.

She trusted God's goodness so deeply that she was ready to hope he would restore what he had taken away.

What great faith!

The One who gave that faith would not disappoint it.

She asked her husband for permission to go immediately to the prophet.

Although she was a woman of rank, she did not rely solely on occasional visits from Elisha to her home.

She also participated in public worship.

God's ministers should ask sincerely about the welfare of their friends and families.

The woman's answer was, “It is well.”

How could everything be well when her child was dead at home?

Everything God does is well ordered.

All is well for those who have died if they have gone to heaven, and all may be well for those who remain if suffering helps them continue toward heaven.

Whenever an earthly comfort is removed, it is well if by grace we can say that our hearts had not made an idol of it.

If we had loved it too much, we have reason to fear it may have been given and removed as discipline.

Elisha prayed to God in faith.

The child was brought back to life and returned to his mother.

People who seek to bring spiritual life to those dead in sin must feel deep concern for them and pray with earnest effort.

No minister can give another person divine life.

Nevertheless, ministers should use every means and work as diligently as though they could.

Harmful food purified and a small meal multiplied (verses 38–44)

There was a famine of bread, but not a famine of hearing God's word.

The sons of the prophets were gathered around Elisha, listening to his teaching.

Elisha made dangerous food wholesome.

If our meal consists of nothing more than a pot of stew, remember that even this great prophet and his guests had no more.

The table can become a trap.

Food that should nourish us may instead bring danger, which is reason to eat with a healthy awareness of our dependence on God.

As we receive life's provisions and comforts, we must remember death's approach and the danger of sin.

We should thank the Lord for making our food healthy and nourishing.

He is the Lord who heals us.

Elisha also made a little food sufficient for many.

What he had freely received, he freely gave.

God has promised his church that he will bless her provisions abundantly and satisfy her poor with bread (Psalm 132:15).

When he provides, his gift is enough.

What he blesses can accomplish a great deal.

Christ's later miracle of feeding the crowds was greater still.

Yet both teach that those who wait upon God while following their duties may trust his providential care.
classic_reading:
[2Kgs.4.1-2Kgs.4.7]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Elisha multiplies the widow's oil. | (1-7) |
The Shunammite obtains a son. | (8-17) |
The Shunammite's son restored to life. | (18-37) |
The miracle of healing the pottage, and of feeding the sons of the prophets. | (38-44) |
Verses 1-7
Elisha's miracles were acts of real charity: Christ's were so; not only great wonders, but great favours to those for whom they were wrought. God magnifies his goodness with his power. Elisha readily received a poor widow's complaint. Those that leave their families under a load of debt, know not what trouble they cause. It is the duty of all who profess to follow the Lord, while they trust to God for daily bread, not to tempt him by carelessness or extravagance, nor to contract debts; for nothing tends more to bring reproach upon the gospel, or distresses their families more when they are gone. Elisha put the widow in a way to pay her debt, and to maintain herself and her family. This was done by miracle, but so as to show what is the best method to assist those who are in distress, which is, to help them to improve by their own industry what little they have. The oil, sent by miracle, continued flowing as long as she had empty vessels to receive it. We are never straitened in God, or in the riches of his grace; all our straitness is in ourselves. It is our faith that fails, not his promise. He gives more than we ask: were there more vessels, there is enough in God to fill them; enough for all, enough for each; and the Redeemer's all-sufficiency will only be stayed from the supplying the wants of sinners and saving their souls, when no more apply to him for salvation. The widow must pay her debt with the money she received for her oil. Though her creditors were too hard with her, yet they must be paid, even before she made any provision for her children. It is one of the main laws of the Christian religion, that we pay every just debt, and give every one his own, though we leave ever so little for ourselves; and this, not of constraint, but for conscience' sake. Those who bear an honest mind, cannot with pleasure eat their daily bread, unless it be their own bread. She and her children must live upon the rest; that is, upon the money received for the oil, with which they must put themselves into a way to get an honest livelihood. We cannot now expect miracles, yet we may expect mercies, if we wait on God, and seek to him. Let widows in particular depend upon him. He that has all hearts in his hand, can, without a miracle, send as effectual a supply.
[2Kgs.4.8-2Kgs.4.17]
Verses 8-17
Elisha was well thought of by the king of Israel for his late services; a good man can take as much pleasure in serving others, as in raising himself. But the Shunammite needed not any good offices of this kind. It is a happiness to dwell among our own people, that love and respect us, and to whom we are able to do good. It would be well with many, if they did but know when they are really well off. The Lord sees the secret wish which is suppressed in obedience to his will, and he will hear the prayers of his servants in behalf of their benefactors, by sending unasked-for and unexpected mercies; nor must the professions of men of God be supposed to be delusive like those of men of the world.
[2Kgs.4.18-2Kgs.4.37]
Verses 18-37
Here is the sudden death of the child. All the mother's tenderness cannot keep alive a child of promise, a child of prayer, one given in love. But how admirably does the prudent, pious mother, guard her lips under this sudden affliction! Not one peevish word escapes from her. Such confidence had she of God's goodness, that she was ready to believe that he would restore what he had now taken away. O woman, great is thy faith! He that wrought it, would not disappoint it. The sorrowful mother begged leave of her husband to go to the prophet at once. She had not thought it enough to have Elisha's help sometimes in her own family, but, though a woman of rank, attended on public worship. It well becomes the men of God, to inquire about the welfare of their friends and their families. The answer was, It is well. All well, and yet the child dead in the house! Yes! All is well that God does; all is well with them that are gone, if they are gone to heaven; and all well with us that stay behind, if, by the affliction, we are furthered in our way thither. When any creature-comfort is taken from us, it is well if we can say, through grace, that we did not set our hearts too much upon it; for if we did, we have reason to fear it was given in anger, and taken away in wrath. Elisha cried unto God in faith; and the beloved son was restored alive to his mother. Those who would convey spiritual life to dead souls, must feel deeply for their case, and labour fervently in prayer for them. Though the minister cannot give Divine life to his fellow-sinners, he must use every means, with as much earnestness as if he could do so.
[2Kgs.4.38-2Kgs.4.44]
Verses 38-44
There was a famine of bread, but not of hearing the word of God, for Elisha had the sons of the prophets sitting before him, to hear his wisdom. Elisha made hurtful food to become safe and wholesome. If a mess of pottage be all our dinner, remember that this great prophet had no better for himself and his guests. The table often becomes a snare, and that which should be for our welfare, proves a trap: this is a good reason why we should not feed ourselves without fear. To the extent that he acted in obedience to God and from right motives, he need not be discouraged by criticism or opposition.

The killing of God's prophets received special attention in the judgment announced.

Jezebel persisted in idolatry and hatred toward Jehovah and his servants until her wrongdoing reached its full measure.

Jehu and the officers (verses 11–15)

People who faithfully bring God's message to sinners have often been dismissed as mad.

Their judgment, language and conduct differ from those of other people.

They are willing to suffer for aims and purposes that worldly people cannot understand.

The accusation is especially often made by the ungodly, who are themselves truly irrational.

By contrast, faithful servants of God demonstrate that their beliefs and actions are wise and reasonable.

Some confidence in God's word seems to have strengthened Jehu for the undertaking before him.

Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah (verses 16–29)

Jehu possessed an intensely energetic temperament.

God's wisdom is seen in the different characters of the people he employs.

Yet being known for fury is no honor to anyone.

A person who rules his own spirit is greater than a mighty warrior.

Joram met Jehu on the land belonging to Naboth.

God sometimes arranges circumstances so that a punishment corresponds strikingly to the crime, as one face reflects another in a mirror.

The path of sin can never become a path of peace (Isaiah 57:21).

What real peace can sinners have with God while they persist in sin?

But when sins are repented of and abandoned, peace is possible.

Joram died under the sentence of divine law.

Ahaziah had bound himself to Ahab's family and become one of them through wrongdoing.

Association with evildoers is dangerous because it entangles us in their guilt and suffering.

Jezebel dies (verses 30–37)

Jezebel did not hide or show fear of God's judgment.

Instead, she continued defiantly to mock the very danger facing her.

A heart hardened against God may resist him boldly to the very end.

Nothing more surely predicts destruction than a heart still proud and unrepentant under circumstances meant to humble it.

Anyone who tempts other people into wickedness or leads them away from truth and righteousness should consider Jezebel's behavior and death.

Jehu called for assistance, and her attendants handed her over.

Thus her life ended.

The destruction of pride and cruelty calls us to acknowledge the Lord's righteousness.

When we indulge bodily desires, remember how perishable the body is.

Soon it will decay, whether beneath the ground or exposed to animals above it.

May we all flee from the divine wrath revealed against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.

Verses 1-10
In these and the like events, we must acknowledge the secret working of God, disposing men to fulfil his purposes respecting them. Jehu was anointed king over Israel, by the Lord's special choice. The Lord still had a remnant of his people, and would yet preserve his worship among them. Of this Jehu was reminded. He was commanded to destroy the house of Ahab, and, as far as he acted in obedience to God, and upon right principles, he needed not to regard reproach or opposition. The murder of God's prophets is strongly noticed. Jezebel persisted in idolatry and enmity to Jehovah and his servants, and her iniquity was now full.
[2Kgs.9.11-2Kgs.9.15]
Verses 11-15
Those who faithfully deliver the Lord's message to sinners, have in all ages been treated as madmen. Their judgment, speech, and conduct are contrary to those of other men; they endure much in pursuit of objects, and are influenced by motives, into which the others cannot enter. But above all, the charge is brought by the worldly and ungodly of all sorts, who are mad indeed; while the principles and practice of the devoted servants of God, prove to be wise and reasonable. Some faith in the word of God, seems to have animated Jehu to this undertaking.
[2Kgs.9.16-2Kgs.9.29]
Verses 16-29
Jehu was a man of eager spirit. The wisdom of God is seen in the choice of those employed in his work. But it is not for any man's reputation to be known by his fury. He that has rule over his own spirit, is better than the mighty. Joram met Jehu in the portion of Naboth. The circumstances of events are sometimes ordered by Divine Providence to make the punishment answer to the sin, as face answers to face in a glass. The way of sin can never be the way of peace, [Isa.57.21] Is 57:21. What peace can sinners have with God? No peace so long as sin is persisted in; but when it is repented of and forsaken, there is peace. Joram died as a criminal, under the sentence of the law. Ahaziah was joined with the house of Ahab. He was one of them; he had made himself so by sin. It is dangerous to join evil-doers; we shall be entangled in guilt and misery by it.
[2Kgs.9.30-2Kgs.9.37]
Verses 30-37
Instead of hiding herself, as one afraid of Divine vengeance, Jezebel mocked at fear. See how a heart, hardened against God, will brave it out to the last. There is not a surer presage of ruin, than an unhumbled heart under humbling providences. Let those look at Jezebel's conduct and fate, who use arts to seduce others to commit wickedness, and to draw them aside from the ways of truth and righteousness. Jehu called for aid against Jezebel. When reformation-work is on foot, it is time to ask, Who sides with it? Her attendants delivered her up. Thus she was put to death. See the end of pride and cruelty, and say, The Lord is righteous. When we pamper our bodies, let us think how vile they are; shortly they will be a feast for worms under ground, or beasts above ground. May we all flee from that wrath which is revealed from heaven, against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men.

Ahab's descendants are killed (verses 1–14)

Even in the most terrible events, including those marked by human crimes, we must acknowledge God's truth and justice.

The Lord never commands anything unjust or unreasonable.

Jehu destroyed the surviving members of Ahab's household who had shared in that family's wickedness.

When we think about the immense amount of human suffering and death, and when we consider the resurrection and final judgment, we may be overwhelmed by the multitude of unrepentant sinners awaiting judgment.

We may ask what ultimately caused all this death and misery.

The answer is sin.

Why then should we welcome sin into our hearts and look for happiness in what has caused so much suffering?

Jehu destroys Baal worship (verses 15–28)

“Is your heart right?”

This is a question we should often ask ourselves.

We may make an impressive profession of faith and gain a good reputation.

But are our hearts truly right before God?

Are we sincere with him?

Jehonadab supported Jehu in both the acts of judgment and religious reform he undertook.

An upright heart is satisfied with God's approval and seeks nothing more.

If our purpose is to win people's applause, our foundation is wrong.

We cannot be sure whether Jehu himself aimed higher than human recognition.

Under the civil law of ancient Israel, idolatry was subject to death.

For the time being, that worship was removed from Israel.

May we desire equally that idolatry be uprooted from our own hearts.

The recorded civil penalty is part of this ancient history, not a command for present-day religious persecution.

Jehu continues in Jeroboam's sin (verses 29–36)

It is right to question whether Jehu acted from a godly principle and whether he made wrong choices even while doing the work of reform.

Nevertheless, God does not leave genuine service rendered to him unrewarded.

True conversion requires turning not only from grossly wicked acts, but from every sin.

It requires abandoning not only false gods, but also false ways of worshiping the true God.

It demands leaving behind not only sins that damage our earthly interests, but also those from which we profit and through which we protect our wealth and standing.

Abandoning profitable sins especially tests our ability to deny ourselves and trust God.

Jehu displayed great zeal for removing false religion.

But he neglected faithful service in true religion.

He did not take care to please God or fulfill his duty.

Where such care is absent, we have reason to fear that saving grace is absent as well.

The people were equally careless.

It is therefore unsurprising that the Lord began to reduce Israel's territory, wealth and strength.

The people had fallen short in their duty toward him, and he caused their nation to fall short in power and prosperity.

Verses 1-14
In the most awful events, though attended by the basest crimes of man, the truth and justice of God are to be noticed; and he never did nor can command any thing unjust or unreasonable. Jehu destroyed all that remained of the house of Ahab; all who had been partners in his wickedness. When we think upon the sufferings and miseries of mankind, when we look forward to the resurrection and last judgment, and think upon the vast number of the wicked waiting their awful sentence of everlasting fire; when the whole sum of death and misery has been considered, the solemn question occurs, Who slew all these? The answer is, SIN. Shall we then harbour sin in our bosoms, and seek for happiness from that which is the cause of all misery?
[2Kgs.10.15-2Kgs.10.28]
Verses 15-28
Is thine heart right? This is a question we should often put to ourselves. I make a fair profession, have gained a reputation among men, but, is my heart right? Am I sincere with God? Jehonadab owned Jehu in the work, both of revenge and of reformation. An upright heart approves itself to God, and seeks no more than his acceptance; but if we aim at the applause of men, we are upon a false foundation. Whether Jehu looked any further we cannot judge. The law of God was express, that idolaters were to be put to death. Thus idolatry was abolished for the present out of Israel. May we desire that it be rooted out of our hearts.
[2Kgs.10.29-2Kgs.10.36]
Verses 29-36
It is justly questionable whether Jehu acted from a good principle, and whether he did not take some false steps in doing it; yet no services done for God shall go unrewarded. But true conversion is not only from gross sin, but from all sin; not only from false gods, but from false worships. True conversion is not only from wasteful sins, but from gainful sins; not only from sins which hurt our worldly interests, but from those that support and befriend them; in forsaking which is the great trial whether we can deny ourselves and trust God. Jehu showed great care and zeal for rooting out a false religion, but in the true religion he cared not, took no heed to please God and do his duty. Those that are heedless, it is to be feared, are graceless. The people were also careless, therefore it is not strange that in those days the Lord began to cut Israel short. They were short in their duty to God, therefore God cut them short in their extent, wealth, and power.
